strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: measuring changes in social bias after continued masked-language-model training. Comparing each retrained model with its pretrained checkpoint is a useful, clearly motivated evaluation target.

Experiments cover four MLMs, two established benchmarks, multiple bias categories, and several existing measures. Worked examples and detailed category-level tables make the empirical results inspectable.

CRR, modified ΔP, and ΔPA recover the intended direction across all 72 reported model–category–training conditions. This provides promising evidence of responsiveness within the controlled retraining setting.
weaknesses: The central accuracy claim needs independent validation. Although Appendix P.1 specifies an 80/20 training/validation split, retraining results are evaluated across the full CPS benchmark, including training examples. After 30 epochs, memorization and adaptation to these examples can explain the strong directional accuracy. Report results on disjoint sentence pairs and include balanced or neutral retraining controls to establish what the metrics specifically detect.

Human alignment provides weak supporting evidence. Figures 4–5 show AUROCs around 0.53–0.57; the best results improve over AUL by only 0.006 for RoBERTa and 0.002 for BERT. With only 58 unbiased versus 1,450 biased pairs and no confidence intervals or significance tests for these differences, superiority is unestablished. Moreover, annotations identify biased text, which does not directly validate the accuracy of model-preference measurements.

The statistical tests do not address the proposed retraining statistic. McNemar’s test compares binary stereotype preferences before and after training, whereas BSRT counts increases in continuous preference gaps. These quantities can behave differently. Consequently, the significance markers do not establish significance of BSRT or greater sensitivity between measures. Appropriate paired inference on preference-gap changes, uncertainty across training runs, and treatment of multiple comparisons are needed.

Equation 10 mishandles ties under the stated directional interpretation. Comparing an unchanged model with itself yields BSRT = 0, although scores below 50 are interpreted as movement toward advantaged-group bias. Explicit neutral treatment of ties and an unchanged-model sanity check are necessary, particularly for discrete rank-based measures.

Claims that other measures underestimate or overestimate bias exceed the available calibration evidence: a higher bias percentage does not itself demonstrate greater accuracy. The construct also needs clarification for StereoSet, where an anti-stereotypical completion need not express bias against an advantaged group; Table 13’s Ethiopian examples illustrate this mismatch.

The contribution of attention weighting is not convincingly isolated. Unweighted ΔP already achieves the same perfect directional accuracy as ΔPA and has higher human-alignment AUROC in both reported models. CRRA changes both the rank transformation and attention weighting relative to CRR, requiring a matched ablation to attribute any benefit to attention.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a clear Findings recommendation. The manuscript omits the optimizer, learning rate, batch size, random seeds, precise split construction, and exact attention aggregation across layers and query/key positions. Although a released package is claimed, no identifying link is provided. These omissions, together with the validation and statistical concerns, warrant revision before acceptance.
